# Perdition Gulch

---

## I.

The land first, because the land was here first and would be here after, and did not care.

Forty-one days without rain and the alkali flats south of town had cracked into a Mosaic of white ruin, each plate curled at its edges like a page refusing to lie flat. The well at the center of Perdition Gulch — the one Hector Strand had dug in sixty-nine, the one they'd stacked with river stone and fitted with a rope so thick a child could climb it — pulled up dust. Not dry mud. Not damp sand promising moisture below. Dust. Fine as milled flour and the same dead grey as the sky, which had not been blue in the memory of anyone who lived there, though that formulation will become complicated shortly, because one of the people who lived there had a memory unlike any instrument yet devised by any civilization on any continent, and even she was beginning to lose confidence in the color of the sky. The cattle — what remained of them, eleven head where once sixty had milled and stamped in Garza's pen — showed their ribs through hide so tightened and thin it looked like sail canvas stretched over the staves of a broken ship. The flies were the last abundant thing. The flies were doing well.

And in this town, which was not a town so much as a scar the desert had not yet finished healing over — fourteen structures, a single street, a population of forty-three souls at rough count, though what constituted a soul in Perdition Gulch was a question the universe was in the process of revisiting — there lived five people who were not like the others.

They were not like the others in quantifiable ways, in demonstrable ways, in ways that had been demonstrated and were known, if not discussed, if not named.

Consider Cora Ellebrecht. Forty-four years old. Born in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, to a family of Lutheran printers who suspected early that something was wrong with their third daughter, because a child who reads a hymnal once at age four and then recites it to the minister backward — backward, beginning with the final amen and ending with the opening invocation, word for word, including the typesetter's error on page forty-one where "salvation" had been printed "slavation" — is either holy or broken, and they were Lutherans, and Lutherans do not traffic in holy.

She had come west because the west did not ask what you could do. It asked what you would do, and these are different questions.

Six months before the well went dry, Sheriff Masson Crane had ridden the nine miles from Saguaro Bend to Perdition Gulch with a wanted poster he'd received by post that morning. He had not shown it to anyone. He had folded it once, placed it inside his vest, and ridden to Cora's cabin because someone in Saguaro Bend had told someone in Lordsburg who had told a cattleman passing through that the woman in the clapboard place at the north end of the gulch could do things with her mind that seemed, to use the cattleman's word, inadvisable. Sheriff Crane was a practical man. He did not believe in witchcraft. He believed in expediency.

He showed her the poster.

She glanced at it. The glance lasted perhaps two seconds — he counted, because he was a man who had learned to count the things that unsettled him, a habit the five would have recognized and respected.

"Anything else?" she asked.

"That's all I came for."

"Ride safe."

He rode back to Saguaro Bend. Six months passed. In that time, the man described on the wanted poster — one James Otero Cardwell, alias Little Jim, alias the Deacon, wanted for murder and mail robbery in the territories — drifted down from Colorado and took a room above the hardware store in Saguaro Bend, using the name Haines. Sheriff Crane did not recognize him. The poster was long since buried in a pile of paper on the office desk, and Crane's memory was an ordinary memory, which is to say it was a sieve.

But on a Tuesday in what the calendar called April and the sky called nothing — no clouds, no color, no opinion — Sheriff Crane rode back to Perdition Gulch. He did not bring the poster this time. He did not need to. He sat on Cora's porch and said, "That paper I showed you. The one from—" and she told him.

She told him the full name, the aliases, the weight (one hundred and seventy-one pounds), the scar (left temple, shaped like a fishhook), the crimes (murder of a postal clerk in Santa Fe, robbery of the Atchison mail in three separate instances), the reward (two hundred and twenty-five dollars, payable upon conviction, by order of the U.S. Marshal's office, the territorial governor's name misspelled on the poster — *Wallce* for Wallace — suggesting it had been typeset locally and in haste). She told it to him backward. Not as a trick, not as theater. She simply began at the end because the end was what he needed — the identification — and worked back toward the description because by then he was asking questions and the answers preceded them in the text.

Sheriff Crane sat very still. Then he said, "Thank you, Cora," and the word *Cora* contained everything the word *ma'am* would have contained if he had been speaking to something he understood.

Consider Drummond. No last name offered and none requested, which was not uncommon in that territory and that decade, where the past was a country many people had emigrated from and did not intend to revisit. Drummond was large in the way that certain weathered things are large — not by height or breadth alone but by density, by the sense that he had been compressed by some force into a shape that took up less space than the material warranted. He was fifty or near it. His hands were the hands of a man who had laid fence and dug wells and pulled calves from dying mothers for thirty years, which he had.

The railroad surveyor came though Perdition Gulch in the spring of eighty-five, part of a crew mapping a spur line that the Southern Pacific believed, and was wrong to believe, would be profitable. The surveyor's name was Aldiss and he had a Bowie knife he kept on his belt and a habit of setting the blade tip-down in whatever table he was eating at, a display of something he imagined was authority. He set the knife in the table of the Garza boarding house and told the six men and two women eating there that the railroad would be coming through and that it might come through their homes and that if it did they would receive fair compensation, which was a lie, and that they should be grateful, which was an opinion.

Drummond was eating a plate of beans.

"That's a fine knife," he said.

Aldiss agreed that it was, and was on the verge of describing how he'd gotten it — a story involving a card game in Abilene that was also a lie, the knife having been ordered from a catalog in St. Louis — when Drummond reached across the table, pulled the knife from the wood, and drove it into his own left thigh.

The sound was not dramatic. The sound was the sound of a blade entering muscle through denim: a muted, wet crunch, domestic almost, like a boot stepping through thin ice on a puddle. The blade went in four inches. Drummond's face registered the entry the way a man's face registers a change in the wind — noticeable, untroubling, already passing.

He looked at Aldiss. He pulled the knife out. And the table saw — all eight of them saw, and two of the eight were among the five and therefore understood what they were seeing and five of the eight were not and therefore did not, and the eighth, Aldiss himself, was too frightened to see anything clearly for the rest of his natural life — the table saw the wound seal itself. Not slowly, not with the cautious granulation of healing flesh over days and weeks. The wound closed the way a mouth closes: a decision was made, and the opening was no longer there. Drummond wiped the blade on his napkin. He set it back in the table.

"You can take the knife," he said. "Leave the spur line."

The spur line did not come through Perdition Gulch. This was attributed to a surveying error.

Consider the child. Peck. Maybe ten and maybe younger, because Peck had arrived in Perdition Gulch at an age too young to articulate his own history and with no adult who could articulate it for him — a child alone on the road, sunburned to the color of old brick, wearing a man's shirt cut down to fit and boots with no soles, found by Cora in 1884 sitting beneath a dead cottonwood as though he had been set there, as though someone had placed him like a package at a way station and ridden on. Cora took him in. Cora named him Peck because when she found him he was pecking at the hardpan with a stick, making small holes, which she later understood were not holes but a kind of notation, because the child was transcribing something, though what he was transcribing was not sound but thought, and the thoughts were not his own.

The cowhand was Daniel Reese, twenty-six, married to a woman named Alma who had stayed behind in Tucson because Daniel Reese had debts he was working to clear and did not want his wife to live in a bunkhouse. Alma had written him a letter. The letter had arrived with the monthly post and Daniel Reese had held it all day and into the night without opening it because he was afraid of what it contained, because he loved his wife and love makes paper dangerous.

Peck sat on the porch of the dry-goods store, which was his customary place, and when Daniel Reese walked past the child said — said quietly, to no one, or to the air, or to whoever was listening from the inside of Daniel Reese's skull where the words lived — "She's not leaving. She got the job at the laundry. She says the winter was hard but the house is warm. She says don't come home until you're ready and not before."

Daniel Reese stopped walking.

The letter was in his back pocket. It had not been opened. The seal — red wax, Alma's thumbprint, a habit of hers — was intact.

He opened it standing in the street.

She had not used those words. She had written in her own way, in sentences that were longer and more careful than the ones Peck had spoken. But the meaning was identical. The *meaning* was what Peck had heard, because what Peck heard was not language but intent, not the sentence but the pressure behind it, the way a dog hears not the word but the tone, except Peck heard tone from a distance of four hundred miles, through sealed wax, through paper, through the skull of a man too frightened to read his own wife's handwriting.

Daniel Reese looked at the child. The child was pecking at the porch rail with a stick. Daniel Reese opened his mouth, then closed it, then walked on. He did not mention the incident. In Perdition Gulch, there were things one did not mention, and this restraint was the rent the townsfolk paid for the privilege of being protected by what they refused to name.

And consider, finally and together, because they could not be considered apart, the twins.

Luz and Lila Obregón. Twenty-eight years old. Born seventeen minutes apart in a room above a cantina in Mesilla, to a mother who survived the birth only to die of fever three weeks later, as though the effort of producing two bodies for a single soul had exhausted the machinery of generation and the debt had to be collected from somewhere. They were identical in face and frame and coloring — dark-eyed, dark-haired, fine-boned in a way that people mistook for fragility and learned not to. They moved through Perdition Gulch on separate errands, at separate ends of town, and held between them a single unbroken field of perception, as though the two skulls were windows in the same room and the room was everywhere.

On a Wednesday — this was a year before the well went dry, in the last months when such demonstrations were still possible without consequence — Luz stood on the steps of the Garza boarding house at the south end of the street and Lila stood in the doorway of Cora's cabin at the north end and a boy named Felix Garza, who was nine and bold and had been told by his mother to stop pestering the twins about their strangeness, held up a playing card behind Lila's back where only Luz, two hundred yards away, could have seen it.

"Seven of clubs," Lila said, without turning.

Felix held up another.

"Queen of hearts."

"She's looking!" Felix shouted. "She's got a mirror!"

But the thing Felix could not accept — the thing he would go to his grave in 1931 not accepting, having moved to California and become a dentist and buried the years in Perdition Gulch so deep in his own ordinary memory that they surfaced only in dreams — was that Lila had not turned and there was no mirror. There was only Luz, two hundred yards south, seeing the card as clearly as Felix himself, and the seeing arriving in Lila's consciousness not as information transmitted but as experience shared, the way a single person sees with two eyes and does not experience it as communication between the left eye and the right but as sight, unified and whole.

They finished each other's sentences. This was the fact the town knew and tolerated and joked about, nervously, the way all human beings joke about the things that frighten them. But the town's understanding was imprecise. They did not finish each other's sentences. They *had* them once. A sentence would begin in Luz's mouth and end in Lila's not because Lila knew what Luz intended but because the intention was singular and the mouths were two, and which mouth a given syllable emerged from was a matter of proximity and convenience, the way a pianist's left hand and right hand are not cooperating but are operated, by a single mind seated behind and above them both.

Not a government. Not a council. Not a coven.

A balance.

This is what the narrator must call it, for lack of a better word in English or Spanish or any of the languages Cora could recall from documents she had read once and never forgotten — *had* never forgotten, a tense that mattered — and the word is imperfect but the imperfection is honest. They balanced the town. Drummond repaired what broke, including bodies, including his own, a gift he could extend to others by closing his hands over a wound and waiting, though this cost him something the narrator does not yet have the vocabulary to describe. Cora knew what needed knowing and remembered what needed remembering, and in a territory where records were scarce and memory was law, this made her a kind of courthouse. Peck heard what people could not say and said it for them, which sounds like a violation and was, sometimes, but was more often a relief, the way a lanced boil is a relief, painful and necessary and better than the alternative. And Luz-Lila — the narrator will use the single name for the single being, though the town never did — Luz-Lila watched. From two positions, from two elevations, from two angles of light and wind and shadow, they watched the perimeter and the interior simultaneously, and nothing entered Perdition Gulch that they did not see, and nothing happened within it that they did not witness, and this fact — this constant, doubled vigilance — was the thing that let the other forty-three souls sleep at night without knowing why they slept easily and without asking.

A balance.

And the well had been dry for forty-one days.

The drought was counted. Everything here was counted.
